evidence.claim: Lehman Caves Road runs west from Baker through desert country toward Great Basin National Park, roughly following Lehman Creek uphill.
evidence.quote: From there, the route travels easterly through desert terrain, roughly paralleling the course of Lehman Creek as it travels down towards the town of Baker.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service directs drivers five miles west on Highway 488 to reach the park.
evidence.quote: In Baker, turn west on Highway 488 and travel five miles to reach the park.

evidence.claim: Nevada’s Department of Transportation designated SR 488 a Nevada Scenic Byway on March 27, 2000.
evidence.quote: The Nevada Department of Transportation designated State Route 488 as a Nevada Scenic Byway on March 27, 2000

evidence.claim: Sagebrush, saltbush, pinyon and Utah juniper dominate the area near the visitor center.
evidence.quote: The area around the Visitor Center is dominated by plants such as sagebrush, saltbush, single-leaf pinyon, and Utah juniper.

evidence.claim: The caves were protected as a national monument in 1922; that monument became part of Great Basin National Park in 1986.
evidence.quote: The Lehman Caves were originally protected as a national monument in 1922, which was combined with the national park in 1986.

evidence.claim: An earlier unimproved route appears on Nevada highway maps by 1937, meeting Baker Road north of town.
evidence.quote: An unimproved road connecting Lehman Caves to the state highway system first appears on official Nevada state highway maps as far back as 1937, although this road traveled more northeasterly than the current alignment of Lehman Caves Road and connected to Baker Road north of the town.

evidence.claim: By 1942, State Route 74 followed the present alignment through Baker; gravel surfacing followed by 1948 and paving by 1949.
evidence.quote: the state's tourist maps did not show the existence of State Route 74 until 1942—by then, the highway route had been changed to its present-day alignment, meeting then-SR 73 at Baker. The new route was upgraded to a gravel road by 1948, and was fully paved by 1949.

evidence.claim: The statewide renumbering replaced SR 74 with SR 488 in 1976.
evidence.quote: SR 74 was eliminated from the state highway system as part of a mass renumbering of Nevada's state routes. State Route 488 was designated to replace SR 74 on July 1, 1976.

evidence.claim: The 1978–79 state highway map was the first to show the new number.
evidence.quote: This change in highway numbers was first seen on the 1978–79 edition of the state highway map.

evidence.quote: SR 488 begins at a cattle guard on Lehman Caves Road, 0.707 miles (1.138 km) east of the Lehman Caves Visitor Center

evidence.claim: Baker sits at the junction of Routes 487 and 488, five miles east of Great Basin National Park’s main entrance.
evidence.quote: It is located 5 miles (8.0 km) east of the main entrance of Great Basin National Park at the junction of State Routes 487 and 488.

evidence.claim: The park’s Great Basin Visitor Center is here on Route 487.
evidence.quote: The Great Basin visitor center is located on Nevada State Route 487 in the town of Baker.

evidence.claim: Inside is a rifle recovered from the park in 2014, leaning against a juniper tree.
evidence.quote: The Forgotten Winchester, a rifle manufactured in 1882 that was found leaning against a juniper tree in the park in 2014, is on display inside the Great Basin visitor center.

evidence.claim: Archaeologist Eva Jensen found the gun during a search for artifacts before a project to reduce wildfire fuels.
evidence.quote: Prior to the rifle's discovery, the National Park Service had started a $280,000 fuels reduction project around Strawberry Creek Campground to prevent campfires from sparking wildfires in the surrounding forest. As part of the project, the Park Service sent staff from their cultural resources office to search the project area for artifacts, and archaeologist Eva Jensen found the rifle

evidence.claim: Manufactured in 1882, the Winchester has no known story explaining its abandonment.
evidence.quote: The gun was manufactured in 1882, but nothing is known of its abandonment.

evidence.claim: X-rays during conservation revealed a cartridge hidden in the buttstock, made between 1887 and 1911.
evidence.quote: the X-rays revealed a live .44-Winchester centerfire caliber cartridge in a compartment inside the buttstock. This cartridge was manufactured by the Union Metallic Cartridge Company sometime between 1887 and 1911.

evidence.claim: The rifle and cartridge are displayed together.
evidence.quote: The rifle is on permanent display in the Baker Visitor Center of Great Basin National Park, along with the cartridge found in it.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service warns that navigation apps can send drivers to remote park locations. Route to Lehman Caves Visitor Center, Great Basin Visitor Center or Baker.
evidence.quote: Do not rely on navigation apps to guide to correct locations. Many will route you incorrectly to extremely remote locations. For best results, route to the "Lehman Caves Visitor Center," the "Great Basin Visitor Center," or to the town of Baker, Nevada.

evidence.claim: Absalom Lehman began guiding visitors into the caves in 1885, but Indigenous people knew them before Europeans arrived.
evidence.quote: The cave had been known to indigenous peoples long before the arrival of Europeans. In 1885, Absalom Lehman, a rancher in the area, began guiding tours into the cave.

evidence.claim: Visitors left inscriptions before the caves became a national monument in 1922.
evidence.quote: Visitors' inscriptions in the cave from the era before it became a National Monument note its use and popularity among recent settlers to the region.

evidence.claim: Near the visitor center, seven apricot trees and one peach tree remain, along with a reconstructed portion of the ditch.
